_about: Arm C provider-call scenarios. Every patient is managed in place; the drill is what the paramedic recommends when calling the primary care provider, and what to arrange after the call.

Same structure and value engine as Arm B (patient card, visit, values from data/bands.json, focus row). Instead of a tier there is an 'ask': a four-option question on the recommendation to the provider.
'call' is a model of how the recommendation is phrased on the phone, shown in feedback. followUp: one four-option question on what happens after the call.
Same construction rules as every other multiple-choice set. All text is U.S. English.

scenarios.title: A supplement nobody prescribed

medications: Potassium gluconate 99 mg tablets, three a day, bought at the pharmacy for leg cramps two weeks ago

social.adherence: Good; adds supplements on advice from friends

visit.reason: Routine visit; new bottle found on the medication check.
visit.history: Feels well. Cramps unchanged. No palpitations or weakness.
visit.vitals: HR 70 regular, BP 132/80, RR 14, SpO2 98% on air
visit.exam: Well. 12-lead ECG: sinus rhythm, no peaked T waves.

ask.stem: What do you recommend to the provider?

options.text: Stop the potassium supplement and recheck in a week
Reduce the lisinopril to 10 mg and recheck in a week
Add a loop diuretic to bring the potassium down
Switch the metformin to a sulfonylurea instead

scenarios.call: "Mr. R, 72, CKD 3a on lisinopril. Potassium today {k}, up from {kb} two months ago; creatinine stable at {cr}. ECG unchanged, asymptomatic. He started over-the-counter potassium tablets two weeks ago for cramps. I'd like to stop the supplement and recheck the potassium in a week. Any changes to the lisinopril?"
scenarios.rationale: Band 1 potassium with an obvious cause: a potassium supplement added on top of an ACE inhibitor in reduced GFR. The ECG is normal and the creatinine has not moved, so nothing is urgent and nothing needs a clinic chair. The supplement is the change; the lisinopril is doing renal and cardiovascular work and there is no reason to touch it when the added potassium explains the rise. A diuretic to chase a supplement would be treating one drug with another.
factors: Rise from a documented baseline with a new potassium source
ECG normal, creatinine unchanged
ACE inhibitor is indicated and not the thing that changed
Over-the-counter product is the fixable cause

followUp.stem: What should the paramedic arrange after the call?

options.text: A potassium recheck in a week and teach-back
A same-day clinic visit to confirm the level
A low-potassium diet sheet and no recheck
A repeat ECG every day for the next week

followUp.rationale: The recheck confirms the supplement was the cause; the teach-back stops the next bottle. He is asymptomatic with a normal ECG, so daily tracings and a clinic visit add nothing.

scenarios.title: Dry on furosemide

patient.living: Lives alone; daughter visits every other day.
diagnoses: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
medications: Furosemide 40 mg twice daily, increased from once daily a month ago after ankle swelling
baselines: Dry weight 64 kg; BUN {bunb} and creatinine {crb} a month ago

visit.reason: Dizzy on standing for a week; near-fall yesterday.
visit.history: Ankle swelling gone. Drinking normally, eating a little less. Passing urine often. No chest pain or breathlessness.
visit.vitals: HR 84, BP 138/78 lying, 112/66 standing with dizziness, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air, weight 61 kg
visit.exam: Dry mucous membranes. No edema. Lungs clear. JVP not raised.

ask.stem: What do you recommend to the provider?

options.text: Stop the losartan and keep the furosemide as it is
Reduce the furosemide back to once daily
Add oral rehydration solution and keep both doses
Hold the metoprolol until the dizziness settles

scenarios.call: "Mrs. T, 83, HFpEF. Furosemide was doubled a month ago for ankle swelling; the swelling has resolved and she is now 3 kg under her dry weight, orthostatic by 26 points with dizziness and a near-fall. BUN {bun} from {bunb}, creatinine {cr} from {crb}, ratio over 20 to 1, sodium normal, lungs clear. I'd like to drop the furosemide back to 40 mg once daily and reweigh in three days."
scenarios.rationale: Over-diuresed: three kilograms under dry weight, orthostatic with symptoms, a BUN-to-creatinine ratio above 20 to 1 with a creatinine drifting up from baseline. The dose increase did its job and is now doing harm. The recommendation is the dose, back to where it was, with a weight and orthostatic recheck; oral fluids on top of an excessive diuretic would be working against the drug, and the metoprolol and losartan are not the cause.
factors: Weight 3 kg below dry weight after a diuretic increase
Symptomatic orthostatic drop with a near-fall
Prerenal pattern: BUN up out of proportion to creatinine
Edema resolved: the reason for the higher dose is gone

followUp.stem: What is the right recheck after the dose change?

options.text: A three-day revisit for weight and orthostatics
A repeat BUN and creatinine in six weeks
A same-day echocardiogram to assess her heart
A daily phone check-in for the next month

followUp.rationale: Weight and standing blood pressure answer the question within days. Six weeks is too long for a patient who nearly fell, and an echocardiogram does not address volume.

scenarios.title: Amiodarone and the INR

medications: Amiodarone 200 mg daily, started three weeks ago by cardiology
baselines: INR {inrb} at the last three checks on the same warfarin dose

visit.history: No bleeding, bruising or falls. No missed doses. Diet unchanged.
visit.vitals: HR 64 irregular, BP 128/76, RR 14, SpO2 98% on air

ask.stem: What do you recommend to the provider?

options.text: Hold warfarin for a week, then restart the same dose
Reduce the warfarin per protocol; recheck in a week
Ask cardiology to stop the amiodarone instead
Continue the current dose and recheck in a month

scenarios.call: "Mr. K, 76, AF on warfarin 5 mg. INR today {inr}, up from a steady {inrb}. No bleeding, no missed doses, diet unchanged; cardiology started amiodarone three weeks ago. I'd like to reduce the warfarin per the anticoagulation protocol and recheck in a week, since the amiodarone effect will keep building."
scenarios.rationale: Band 1: up to 0.5 above the target with no bleeding is a dose adjustment per protocol and a recheck, a leave-at-home decision. The cause is amiodarone, which raises the INR and whose effect grows for weeks, so the right ask is a modest dose reduction now with a recheck, not a one-month wait and not a week off the drug, which would leave an atrial fibrillation patient unprotected. The amiodarone is cardiology's decision and is doing its own job.
factors: INR above target but under 3.6, no bleeding
Clear interacting drug started three weeks ago
Amiodarone's effect on warfarin is still increasing
Adjustment available by phone order per protocol

followUp.stem: What should the paramedic tell him about the amiodarone?

options.text: The warfarin will need more adjustment as it builds
He should stop it if the INR is high again next week
It has no further effect on the INR after three weeks
He should take it at a different time from the warfarin

followUp.rationale: Amiodarone accumulates over weeks to months, so the INR will need more than one adjustment; timing does not change the interaction, and stopping a cardiology drug is not the patient's or the paramedic's call.

scenarios.title: Metformin at the creatinine cutoff

visit.reason: Routine visit with a metabolic panel requested by the clinic.
visit.history: Feels well. Eating and drinking normally. No nausea, no vomiting.
visit.vitals: HR 74, BP 130/78, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air

ask.stem: What do you recommend to the provider?

options.text: Continue the metformin; the rise is only mild
Hold the lisinopril and continue the metformin
Stop the metformin; choose a replacement agent
Halve the amlodipine to protect her kidneys

scenarios.call: "Mrs. L, 74, type 2 diabetes with CKD 3b. Creatinine today {cr}, up from {crb} six months ago and now above the 1.4 mg/dL cutoff for a woman on metformin. She is well, fasting glucose {glu}, HbA1c {a1cb}. I'd like to stop the metformin and ask you to choose a replacement, and to repeat the creatinine in two weeks."
scenarios.rationale: The long-standing metformin contraindication is a creatinine at or above 1.5 mg/dL in men and 1.4 mg/dL in women, and she has crossed it. The rise is gradual, under 25% from baseline, in a well patient, so this is a phone call and a regimen decision, not an evaluation. The lisinopril is renoprotective and stays; amlodipine has nothing to do with the kidney. The provider chooses what replaces the metformin.
factors: Creatinine above the sex-specific metformin cutoff
Gradual rise, well patient, normal glucose
Lisinopril indicated for diabetic kidney disease
Regimen replacement is a prescriber decision

followUp.stem: What should the paramedic do about her glucose monitoring once the metformin stops?

options.text: Extra fingerstick checks, reviewed at the next visit
Stop checking; the HbA1c will guide the replacement
Urine ketone checks twice a day for two weeks
A sliding-scale insulin sheet from the vehicle kit

followUp.rationale: Stopping a glucose-lowering drug needs closer readings until the replacement is settled. Ketone checks are for illness, and insulin plans are the prescriber's.

scenarios.title: Drowsy on gabapentin

medications: Gabapentin 600 mg three times daily, increased from 300 mg two months ago
baselines: eGFR {egfr} on the last two panels

social.mobility: Walker since a near-fall last month

patient.goals: Wants to stay in his apartment

visit.reason: Son concerned about daytime sleepiness and unsteadiness.
visit.history: Sleepy most afternoons since the gabapentin increase. Foot pain better. Unsteady, one near-fall. No confusion at night, no new medications otherwise.
visit.vitals: HR 70, BP 134/78 lying, 130/76 standing, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air
visit.exam: Drowsy but oriented. Mild ataxia on tandem walk. No focal deficit.

ask.stem: What do you recommend to the provider?

options.text: Reduce the gabapentin, given his eGFR and the sedation
Stop the amlodipine to correct the unsteadiness
Add a morning stimulant to offset the sleepiness
Keep the dose; the neuropathy pain has improved

scenarios.call: "Mr. B, 81, CKD 3a with eGFR {egfr}. Gabapentin was doubled to 1,800 mg a day two months ago; since then he is drowsy every afternoon, ataxic, and had a near-fall. Creatinine {cr}, glucose {glu}, not orthostatic. Gabapentin clears renally, so I'd like to reduce the dose and reassess in two weeks."
scenarios.rationale: Gabapentin accumulates as clearance falls, and 1,800 mg a day at an eGFR in the 40s and 50s is a sedating dose. The sedation and ataxia arrived with the increase and he has already nearly fallen. The eGFR is the number that governs dosing here; it is stable and not a disposition question. Amlodipine is not the cause and he is not orthostatic. Pain control is real but a fall would cost him the apartment.
factors: Sedation and ataxia began with the dose increase
Renally cleared drug at reduced eGFR
Near-fall in a man living alone
Not orthostatic; blood pressure is not the cause

followUp.stem: What should the paramedic set up before leaving?

options.text: A falls referral and a revisit in two weeks
A same-day neurology consultation for the ataxia
Bed rest at home until the drowsiness clears
A home glucose monitor for nightly checks

followUp.rationale: The dose change addresses the cause; the referral and revisit address the risk in the meantime. Bed rest deconditions him, and neither neurology nor glucose checks fit the picture.

scenarios.title: Ten years of omeprazole

medications: Omeprazole 40 mg daily for ten years
baselines: Magnesium never checked until this week

visit.reason: Review of send-out results drawn for leg cramps and fatigue.
visit.history: Cramps most nights, tired. No palpitations, no diarrhea. Reflux well controlled; has not tried a lower dose in years.
visit.vitals: HR 72 regular, BP 126/74, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air

ask.stem: What do you recommend to the provider?

options.text: Oral magnesium replacement and an omeprazole review
An increase in the furosemide to clear the cramps
Potassium replacement alone, rechecked in a month
A switch from carvedilol to another beta-blocker

scenarios.call: "Mrs. D, 69, on omeprazole 40 mg for ten years plus furosemide. Magnesium {mg}, potassium {k} down from {kb}, nightly cramps, ECG normal. I'd like oral magnesium replacement and a plan to step the omeprazole down, and I'll recheck both electrolytes in two weeks."
scenarios.rationale: A long-term proton pump inhibitor with a loop diuretic is the classic magnesium-depleting pair, and the potassium is falling with it, which is what refractory hypokalemia looks like before anyone has tried to replace the potassium. Magnesium band 2 is a provider consult with an ECG, and the ECG is normal. Replacing potassium alone would fail; the magnesium comes first, and the cause is the omeprazole dose nobody has revisited in a decade.
factors: Low magnesium with a falling potassium
PPI plus loop diuretic: the named depleting combination
Symptomatic but ECG normal
Omeprazole dose never reviewed

followUp.stem: What should be rechecked, and when?

options.text: Both electrolytes together in about two weeks
Potassium alone, rechecked in three months
A 12-lead ECG each day for the coming week
Magnesium alone, after the omeprazole is reduced

followUp.rationale: Both electrolytes move together and both are being treated; two weeks shows whether replacement is working. The ECG was normal and does not need daily repetition.

scenarios.title: Thiazide, SSRI, and a quiet sodium

medications: Sertraline 100 mg daily, dose increased six weeks ago

visit.reason: Scheduled visit; sodium rechecked after the antidepressant change.
visit.history: Feels well. Mood better. No nausea, headache, confusion or falls.
visit.vitals: HR 72, BP 136/80, RR 14, SpO2 98% on air
visit.exam: Alert, fully oriented. Neurological exam normal. Well hydrated.

ask.stem: What do you recommend to the provider?

options.text: Stop the sertraline, since the SSRI is the cause
Restrict her fluid intake to one liter a day
Swap the thiazide for another antihypertensive
No change; recheck the sodium in three months

scenarios.call: "Mrs. P, 70, on hydrochlorothiazide, sertraline increased six weeks ago. Sodium {na}, down from {nab}, asymptomatic, neuro exam normal. A thiazide and an SSRI together are the likely cause. Her mood is finally stable, so I'd suggest swapping the thiazide for another antihypertensive and rechecking the sodium in two weeks."
scenarios.rationale: An asymptomatic band 1 sodium with a documented fall of about eight points after an SSRI increase in a patient already on a thiazide: two drugs that both lower sodium. Nothing here is urgent. The question is which drug to change, and the answer is the one whose job can be done by something else. Her depression has just stabilized on the sertraline; the thiazide has half a dozen substitutes. Fluid restriction treats the number rather than the cause.
factors: Sodium fallen from baseline but band 1 and asymptomatic
Two sodium-lowering drugs, one recently increased
Sertraline is working and hard to replace
Thiazide is easily substituted

followUp.stem: What symptom teaching does she need before the recheck?

options.text: Report headache, nausea, confusion or unsteadiness
Weigh herself each morning and report gains
Cut back on salt until the sodium recovers
Call if her mood dips at all after the tablet change

followUp.rationale: The danger of hyponatremia is neurological, so those are the symptoms that matter. Salt avoidance would worsen it, weight is not the issue, and the sertraline is not being changed.

scenarios.title: Titrating lactulose by phone

baselines: Ammonia {nh3b} at the last clinic visit, oriented
Usual bowel pattern on lactulose: two to three soft stools a day

visit.reason: Wife reports 'he seems a bit slow' and is constipated.
visit.history: One hard stool in three days. Taking the lactulose as prescribed. Slightly slow to answer, no confusion, sleeping normally. No vomiting, no black stools, no fever.
visit.vitals: HR 74, BP 120/74, RR 14, SpO2 97% on air, temp 36.8 °C
visit.exam: Oriented to person, place and date. No asterixis. Abdomen soft, mildly distended, non-tender.

labs.label: Ammonia (send-out from yesterday's clinic draw, reported by phone)

ask.stem: What do you recommend to the provider?

options.text: Increase the lactulose toward two or three soft stools
Add a daily stimulant laxative instead of more lactulose
Restrict protein until the ammonia comes back down
Increase the spironolactone to reduce the distension

scenarios.call: "Mr. S, 64, cirrhosis with prior encephalopathy. One hard stool in three days on lactulose 20 mL twice daily, slightly slow but oriented, no asterixis, no bleeding. Ammonia {nh3} from {nh3b}. He is under his target of two to three soft stools. I'd like to increase the lactulose to three times daily and titrate to the stool count, with a revisit in two days."
scenarios.rationale: Lactulose is dosed to stools, not to milliliters or to an ammonia level, and he is under his target. Grade 1 slowing with constipation and a clean exam is band 1: a care-plan adjustment made by phone. The number is barely above his baseline and does not decide anything; the stool count does. Protein restriction is obsolete and harmful, and spironolactone is for ascites, not bowels.
factors: Below his stool target on the current dose
Oriented, no asterixis, no bleeding, no infection
Constipation is the commonest precipitant and the easiest to fix
Ammonia level is not the treatment target

followUp.stem: What should the wife be taught to track?

options.text: The daily stool count against his target
The ammonia result from each clinic visit
His weight on the scale each morning
The number of lactulose doses he refuses

followUp.rationale: Stool count is the titration target and the early-warning sign. Ammonia correlates poorly with encephalopathy, and weight tracks ascites, not bowels.

scenarios.title: Lows before dawn

medications: Insulin glargine 40 units at bedtime, increased from 34 units a month ago

visit.reason: Wife reports sweats and nightmares; fasting readings have dropped.
visit.history: Log shows fasting readings of 58–68 mg/dL on four of the last seven mornings, one 3 am reading of 55. Daytime readings 120–160. Eating normally, no illness, no alcohol.
visit.vitals: HR 72, BP 128/76, RR 14, SpO2 98% on air

ask.stem: What do you recommend to the provider?

options.text: Cut the glargine by 10–20%; review the log weekly
Move the glargine to the morning at the same dose
Add a bedtime snack and keep the dose unchanged
Stop the insulin and restart metformin instead

scenarios.call: "Mr. V, 67, type 2 diabetes on glargine 40 units at night since a dose increase a month ago. Four fasting lows under 70 this week, one at 3 am of 55, night sweats. Fasting today {glu}, daytime readings 120–160, HbA1c {a1cb}, creatinine {cr} stable. Overnight hypoglycemia from the basal dose; I'd suggest reducing the glargine by 10 to 20 percent and I'll review his log in a week."
scenarios.rationale: Recurrent fasting and nocturnal lows a month after a basal insulin increase, with daytime readings in range and an HbA1c that is already acceptable, means the basal dose is too high. Band 1 glucose: treat and recheck, and the recheck here is a dose change. A snack treats the symptom and adds calories; moving the timing does not reduce the total; and stopping insulin for metformin, in a patient with CKD, is not a phone decision.
factors: Pattern of fasting and nocturnal lows after a dose increase
Daytime readings in range; HbA1c acceptable
Reliable log makes the pattern clear
Basal dose is the single variable that changed

followUp.stem: What should the couple be taught before the dose change takes effect?

options.text: How to treat a low and when to check at 3 am
To skip the glargine on nights he eats less
To check the pen dial and dose as prescribed
To cut fingersticks back to once a week

followUp.rationale: Treating a low correctly and confirming the overnight pattern are the safety net. Skipping doses on judgment and reducing monitoring are the opposite of what the week needs.

scenarios.title: Swollen ankles, normal BNP

medications: Amlodipine 10 mg daily, increased from 5 mg six weeks ago
baselines: BNP {bnpb} two years ago during a work-up that found no heart failure
Weight 70 kg at the last visit

visit.reason: Ankle swelling for a month; she asks whether she needs 'a water pill.'
visit.history: Bilateral ankle swelling since the amlodipine increase. No breathlessness, no orthopnea, sleeps flat. Weight unchanged.
visit.vitals: HR 70, BP 126/74, RR 14, SpO2 98% on air, weight 70 kg
visit.exam: Bilateral pitting ankle edema. Lungs clear. JVP not raised. No hepatomegaly.

ask.stem: What do you recommend to the provider?

options.text: Add furosemide 20 mg daily for the edema
Reduce the amlodipine or switch to another agent
Order an echocardiogram before any change
Compression stockings and no medication change

scenarios.call: "Mrs. G, 73, amlodipine increased to 10 mg six weeks ago; bilateral ankle edema since. No orthopnea, weight unchanged, lungs clear, JVP normal, BNP {bnp} against a baseline of {bnpb}, creatinine {cr}. This looks like calcium-channel-blocker edema rather than heart failure. I'd suggest going back to 5 mg or switching agents rather than adding a diuretic."
scenarios.rationale: Dose-related ankle edema from a dihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker, with a normal BNP against her own baseline, no weight gain, clear lungs and a normal JVP. The lab is one input, and here it supports what the exam already says. A diuretic would treat a drug side effect with another drug and dehydrate a woman who is not overloaded; stockings leave the cause in place. An echocardiogram is not needed to change a dose.
factors: Edema began with the amlodipine increase
No signs of heart failure on exam or weight
BNP normal and at her baseline
Dose reduction or substitution removes the cause

followUp.stem: What should the paramedic check at the follow-up visit?

options.text: Blood pressure and whether the edema is receding
A repeat BNP to confirm the diagnosis was right
Daily weights looking for fluid overload signs
A 12-lead ECG to look for a new arrhythmia

followUp.rationale: The dose change trades edema for blood pressure control, so both are checked. The BNP was already normal, and there was no overload to track.
